name: Xu Zhou (Lukas)
headline: I turn ideas into live products, end to end.
tagline: Xu Zhou (Lukas) builds products from idea to launch, combining product judgment, AI-assisted engineering, and data science. Explore selected apps, AI workflows, and the decisions behind them.
bio: I combine product judgment, AI-assisted engineering, and data science to build useful consumer apps. I own the journey from the first product decision to the data model, the experience, and the launch.

featured.title: Car TCO Compare
featured.oneLiner: A free calculator that compares up to six cars on five-year total cost of ownership, loads real listings, and emails TCO-ranked deal alerts.
featured.problem: Car buyers anchor on sticker price or monthly payment, but total cost of ownership decides the real bill. Existing TCO tools are black boxes locked to specific trims; they will not put arbitrary cars side by side under your own holding period, mileage and financing.
featured.built: A no-sign-up static app: 1 to 6 new or used cars (gas, hybrid, EV) on a fully editable 7-line TCO, answer-first output with a winner banner, a stacked cost breakdown per car and a cumulative-cost chart. "Load a real car" pulls from a bundled snapshot of 1,420 real 2020-and-newer listings (dated 2026-06-22, refreshed annually). A "Deal Alerts" email backend watches new listings and sends a TCO-ranked digest.
featured.how: React, TypeScript and Vite on GitHub Pages. The calculation engine is a pure function with no DOM or I/O imports, reused in a second app. Listings are an API snapshot shipped with the build and refreshed by a scheduled GitHub Action. The alerts backend is Supabase Postgres with row-level security, a Deno Edge Function, transactional email through Resend with idempotent double opt-in, on a daily GitHub Actions cron. Built with AI coding agents under my direction; the orchestrated crew process came with the next two apps. Everything runs on free tiers.
featured.outcome: Live at $0/month, pre-revenue. A paid alerts tier is designed but deliberately not launched: it would need a commercial listings-data license first, and I would rather show that blocker than hide it. Next: per-rate estimate labels in the UI and real cost data to replace the illustrative segment rates.
honest: 42 Vitest tests on the engine, depreciation curve, vehicle resolver and listings loader; the formulas are written down in [docs/design/tco-model.md](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-tco-compare/blob/main/docs/design/tco-model.md).
The app's footer states that its cost assumptions are illustrative segment-level estimates; resale and registration are marked est. The value is the relative ranking under your own assumptions.

The alerts backend keeps a public [run log](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-tco-compare/blob/main/rav4-alert/RUN_LOG.md) and its pre-ship [review findings](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-tco-compare/blob/main/rav4-alert/review-findings.md); the daily cron had 12 consecutive green runs as of 2026-09-30.
Listings are a best-effort snapshot from the Auto.dev API (free tier); verify before buying.
featured.caption: Figures shown are illustrative estimates; the app states its cost assumptions are illustrative. Listings: Auto.dev snapshot.
featured.caveat: Source is public under the PolyForm Noncommercial license.

featured.title: Multi-Agent Build Orchestrator
featured.oneLiner: A reusable workflow that turns a product brief into coordinated work for specialized AI agents, with integration checks, decision records, and release verification.

visual.title: From Brief to Release
visual.caption: Workflow illustration · human direction and review

featured.problem: Building with several AI agents creates coordination work: agreeing on interfaces, managing dependencies, resolving conflicting changes, and deciding whether the result actually meets the brief.
featured.built: A reusable orchestration workflow with a product-manager session, nine specialist roles, shared artifact templates, and explicit acceptance criteria. The main session scopes the work and chooses which specialists are needed; it does not launch a full crew for every small change.
featured.how: The orchestrator sequences dependent tasks and assigns separate implementation areas to parallel agents. Shared contracts guide the build, integration checks connect the parts, and reviewers inspect the result before release. Run logs, decision records, and project state make the work traceable. I direct the brief and the consequential decisions.
featured.outcome: Used to build Car Shopping and Apartment Shopping and support the Car TCO Compare alerts backend. The workflow is reusable across projects; this public case study describes the approach while the implementation remains private.
honest: The public Car Shopping and Apartment Shopping repositories include build logs, decision records, and review findings linked in their case studies below.
Agents assist implementation; the workflow does not remove the need for product judgment, code review, or live verification.
No measured claim of time saved, quality improvement, or fully autonomous delivery is made here.

featured.title: AI Usage Tracker
featured.oneLiner: A local Windows dashboard for AI subscription usage and reset times, designed to make remaining allowance, stale readings, and connection status clear at a glance.

visual.title: AI Usage Tracker
visual.caption: Capability illustration · no account or usage data

featured.problem: Working across AI tools means checking separate usage limits, reset windows, and dashboards. A missing or stale reading can easily look like available capacity unless the interface makes uncertainty explicit.
featured.built: A Windows sidebar and browser dashboard with separate quota windows, reset countdowns, usage history, connection details, and settings. The desktop launcher starts the local service and restores the existing app when opened again.
featured.how: Provider adapters normalize observations into a common model while preserving source timestamps and units. A local server stores account usage on the device, and the Electron shell hosts the same interface as the browser. Codex uses its installed account interface; Claude has a status-line bridge; Cursor uses a paired browser extension. Unknown and expired values remain explicit.
featured.outcome: The local app is usable and Codex readings have been reconciled against the provider source. Claude still awaits a live quota event, and Cursor extension installation and live reconciliation remain pending. This case study shows capabilities without exposing account data or linking to the source repository.
honest: Codex has a verified live reading. Claude and Cursor are incomplete integrations, not confirmed live connections.
Subscription names and prices are user-entered; they do not establish quota size or change billing.
The visual is a capability illustration, not a screenshot of a connected account. No real percentages, identifiers, or reset times are published.
This is a tool for managing AI usage; its dashboard does not run an AI model.

featured.title: Car Shopping
featured.oneLiner: A used-car shortlist that raises risk flags, tracks features honestly, and ranks candidates by estimated cost of ownership instead of sticker price.
featured.problem: Shopping for a used hybrid SUV with a deadline, I had listings scattered across five sites with inconsistent wording. Sticker price is a poor way to rank near-identical cars: the cheaper one can depreciate faster, carry rental-fleet mileage, or hide an accident.
featured.built: A private, static board for every candidate: photo, price and estimated out-the-door, an estimated N-year cost to own, a ten-feature row that is explicitly has / confirmed absent / unknown, and automatic flags such as branded title, accidents, prior theft, high miles per year, no service records and over-market price. Filter, sort by cost of ownership, compare side by side, and push the shortlist straight to a Google Sheet. Listings were captured from screenshots with an AI assistant into a typed seed file; the app itself does no scraping.
featured.how: React, TypeScript and Vite with only two runtime dependencies. A frozen types contract, a pure domain engine with no React imports, and a thin UI that only renders. The TCO engine is vendored from Car TCO Compare with a written decision record on why. Google Sheets sync goes through an Apps Script web app with no server, no OAuth client and no secret in the bundle. First app built with my orchestrated agent crew: a product-manager session, a build brief I confirm, nine role agents, approval gates I sign off on.
featured.outcome: Built for my own 18-car search. Single-user by design, with state in the browser. Next: package the shared TCO engine instead of vendoring it.
honest: 211 Vitest tests lock the flag rules, derived math, the Sheets export matrix and the TCO engine; a type-check gates every build.

The build left its receipts in the repo: [RUN_LOG](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-shopping/blob/main/RUN_LOG.md), [DECISIONS](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-shopping/blob/main/DECISIONS.md), [STATE](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-shopping/blob/main/STATE.md) and a pre-ship [review](https://github.com/xzhou110/car-shopping/blob/main/review-findings.md).
Cost figures are estimates and labelled Est. in the app; the value is in the relative ranking.

featured.title: Apartment Shopping
featured.oneLiner: A rental shortlist that brings lease fit, distance, risk flags, and search progress into one place, from first look to final decision.
featured.problem: Hunting a short-term Bay Area lease across Zillow, Craigslist, Apartments.com and building sites, browser tabs and spreadsheets lost context: no photos, no distance to what mattered, no record of what had been contacted, toured or ruled out.
featured.built: One board for candidates. Each listing shows rent against an estimated market comp, beds, baths, square feet, availability and lease term, with flags for possible scam, income restriction, lease fit against the goal, over- or under-market rent and stale listings. Red flags always sort first. Distance from a chosen anchor is resolved offline for 429 Bay Area ZIPs and 106 neighborhoods. Compare side by side, export to Google Sheets. Listings are hand-curated into a seed file; there is no automated import.
featured.how: The same architecture as Car Shopping, matured: all domain logic (flags, distance, geocoding, filters, export) is pure functions with an injectable clock. Persistence is a committed seed catalog plus a localStorage overlay with migration-safe stable ids, so retiring a listing never wipes the user's notes. Deployed by GitHub Actions to Pages. Built with the same agent crew and the same approval gates.
featured.outcome: Built for my own search. Single-user by design. Next: component tests (the suite covers the engine, not the UI) and driving-time distance instead of straight-line.
honest: 300 Vitest tests across the flag, distance, derive, format and export modules, plus a written [test report](https://github.com/xzhou110/apartment-shopping/blob/main/docs/test-report.md) and [review findings](https://github.com/xzhou110/apartment-shopping/blob/main/docs/review-findings.md).
Scam and income-restriction flags are set by hand at capture time, not detected automatically; market comps are my estimates; distance is straight-line.

howIBuild.intro: AI agents help me execute. The product decisions, trade-offs, and standard of evidence stay with me.

steps.title: Frame the Decision
steps.body: Start with a real problem. Define who it serves, what they need to decide, and the smallest useful product. Make cost, data, and architecture trade-offs explicit.

steps.title: Direct the Build
steps.body: Turn the brief into clear contracts for specialized AI agents. Keep core calculations separate from the interface, review the code, and document the decisions.

steps.title: Verify and Learn
steps.body: Test the logic, check the experience, and verify the deployed app. Label estimates, record limitations, and turn useful lessons into reusable workflows.
